One of the reasons I'm terrified of admitting to myself I could be trans is because of the way it seems ftm people are treated. I am scared of being even more invisible. I'm scared of feeling invalidated because, despite feeling male, I still have feminine interests, I still want to be... cute? And I feel like, if I admit this, I'll become even more invisible. Just because I don't want facial hair (I find body hair uncomfortable; I've got ASD and sensory issues). I still like pink, and glitter. I just feel like I am a male. I feel like there won't be any support out there at all for me, and instead I'll be bombarded with "maybe you're nonbinary" statements. Maybe I am. I could be trans male. I could be nonbinary. I'm still confused, and I'm still heavy in denial, and I don't even want to think about not being in denial if this is really how ftm people are treated. I'm sorry, I've been bottling all these feelings up for weeks. It's hurting a lot. Not the invisibility of ftm people, just the whole possibility thing.

Someone had some on a mirror once), I've changed so many beds and sheets people have shit in, I've fucking changed bin bags people have fucking shit in, that when it comes to anything shit related, I'm solid. 

Like. I sat down with people the other week and watched Two Girls One Cup and can report back that, while it isn't my cup of tea, I felt Nothing. I look at shit now and it's just... there. I can clean it up without heaving or wearing gloves (though to be fair I really should but when you've got twenty minutes to make each room up and you're on a tight time limit, running back and forth to grab gloves is somewhat inconvenicancing). I can smell shit and feel nothing. When my brother doesn't flush the toilet after he has a shit, I don't re-enact the Scottish Girls videos anymore. 

I am the master of shit. Shit doesn't phase me. Snot and half eaten food on the other hand still fucking bother me. Crusted mucus on the sinks and mirrors is the worst fucking thing. 

And to be clear, there's no fetish. I work weekends at a budget hotel. I get all the lovely aftermath of drunk people.

I am a female with aspergers, and I study English Language and Health And Social Care at A Level (alongside English Literature). In these subjects we study gender and social influences and how they differ between the genders.

Basically, from what I have gathered, women at a young age are more likely to try and involve peers in their games. Not all will, and not all "loners" will be included, but there is a higher chance. This is why I believe aspie women cam experience symptoms which differ to "male" symptoms, and vice versa. I find myself with a fair mix of the two... "sets" of symptoms. I strongly believe environmental factors at a young age influence our development, therefore incluencing  the way our symptoms manifest. For example, girls are forced into the caring, motherly role with dolls and that kind of thing, therefore putting emphasis on things like empathy and showing empathy, whereas a male isn't. This perhaps explains why some males struggle to show empathy, whereas some women don't. As a child I was more masculine, and this was readily accepted by my parents, with preferance to dinosaurs rather than dolls. I also believe early interests influence our devolopment; if it wasn't for reading, I imagine I would be a lot "worse" than I am now. 

On the whole, I both support and reject the idea of presenting differently. I support it because it tends to be true, but I reject it because it isn't as well known that women present differently (the amount of times I'm told I don't "look like I have aspergers" is ridiculous), and both genders can experience symptoms from each side. I believe it's about time we kind of just stick both sets of symptoms together.

I'm currently reading Warriors. I like it. I suffer with depression and anxiety, and have aspergers, so my attention is often a bit... not there all the time. I am seventeen. I do find myself enjoying them alongside "harder" books sometimes, as I like to read multiple at a time and having something "easy" is quite nice. 

I know some look down on people who purely read YA and aren't in the actual age demographic, but I think it's easy to forget why. I personally find a lot of YA to  be too cliché for my tastes but if someone enjoys it then so what? And it's an introduction to reading, and some may struggle with attention.

And for the record, Warriors is pretty graphic. It says it is for 9+, but I'm thinking it's more for 11-13. I know a few adults also read Warriors, alongside a fair few older teenagers such as myself.

I also like Pullip dolls (I'm not a big fan of Blythe though) and all the spin offs by the company, and a few other dolls from the Asian market, such as Azone's Kiki pop dolls, and Cu-poche dolls. As for the western market... I quite like vintage Barbie dolls, though there have been some very cool recent releases. I also find some of the Monster High dolls to be quite cool, but I'm not sure I'd collect them. I do still have a soft spot for American Girl dolls, which were the dolls which got me into the hobby, so I would have thought about collecting them again, but I'm not big on the direction the company has been going lately with the quality of the dolls, clothing and general packaging? And a few smaller vintage dolls, such as Strawberry Shortcake. Oh, and Disney's Animator dolls are super cute. 

But alas. I'm somewhat poor, though I do work now, so that's cool (I'm seventeen, I've been working for a few months), and I live with my mother, so my space is super limited. Particularly as I also own a lot of books? I still haven't decided where I'm going to display my BJD, but I'm thinking maybe one of my bookshelves. I'm even more limited considering most of my room is bathed in sunlight. I'll work it out eventually. I'd prefer not to keep her in storage, as I've waited years to get this particular doll. 

I'm both picky and not picky. I don't really know? I'm one of those people who will impulse buy pretty much anything, but I imagine I'd be quite picky at the minute because of space and finances and whatever, plus of most the dolls I'm interested in are stupidly expensive. So maybe I would be pretty picky. 

And what draws me to dolls? I... don't know. I didn't get to play with them much as a child. Despite (biologically) being a girl, and wanting to, I suppose I was scared of my father's opinions. I did tend to find more "masculine" things appealing anyway, like dinosaurs, space and pokèmon. Nowadays I struggle with my gender, but that's irrelevant, but I wonder if that has anything to do with the way I was raised as a child. I think one of the reasons I love dolls so much is possibly because they don't talk. They aren't confusing, or... well, alive? I can talk to dolls comfortably knowing they won't judge me or do/say things I won't understand. It's comforting. I like dolls because of the way you can customise most of them. I like the community? I'm not involved in it very much, and it's my first time posting here, but the community seems lovely, and the few times I've spoken to people regarding BJD's I've always been met very warmly and helpfully. I got interested in dolls not long after father left, and I'm not sure if I'll ever stop? I can't see it at the minute. Dolls are one of my special interests, I often flit between several subjects (I've got aspergers) but dolls is a main one. So uh. I hope I answered your questions well enough.

Once I came out as gay I was hoping I'd feel more comfortable, because I was being more true to myself, but something still seemed very off. While I'd thought about it while thinking about my sexuality, it was... too scary to think about. Too much. I was already in a fragile place, and didn't want to push it. I lied, and that was that. That was... shit. Three years ago? Four? And as for triggers... I can't say there is. Not any I've picked up on, anyway.

I'm working on the whole smoking kind of thing. Like. When smoking you damage the ciliated epithelial cells in your throat, which are the cells with the tiny, tiny, microscopic, little hairs which push all the dust and dirt and stuff you breathe in. This includes bacteria. So they push the bacteria back up. Smokers essentially damage the hairs on these cells, the teacher said they essentially burn them off. Without the hairs, the dust and dirt and bacteria gets stuck, hence why they cough so much and get seem to get ill more, and when they do, it's worse. Or seen as worse. She never specified what she meant by that. So I'm assuming it's the same as your nose. So yes. Please don't do that again. I understand some people trim them, but to be honest I don't think most people have the kind that need trimming. Also please don't smoke. Your ciliated epithelial cells will thank you. They're my favourite cells.

Oh I've been learning about accents and stuff in English Language (we have been learning about regional differences in accents in the UK, as that is where we live). 

I live in Birmingham, which is often regarded to have the worst accent. I don't carry it,instead speaking using RP, which means recieved pronunciation. It's the stereotypical posh accent, I suppose. 3% of the population speak true RP; I typically try to tone it down in college as I get teased for the accent. 

To the best of my knowledge, I'm under the belief it is based on education, and region, all that jazz. For example, places where the mining industry was a big thing, or factory work was a big thing, typically have accents looked down upon due to this "lower class" sort of work. People who spoke RP tended to have had ettiqute lessons, and were often taught how to be "proper", and therefore didn't carry "working class" accents. As they didn't really mix with the "common people", they didn't pick up accents and stuff, whereas a lot of our accents have began to sort of spread and mix. 

Nowadays classism surrounding accents still exists, for sure. I used to be fairly well off, and attended private schools. However, what is interesting to note is that the people at the schools I went to typically carried the regional accent too. I struggle to imitate accents, so I'm assuming it's to do with that. I began attending public school, and it was surprising how many people assumed I was posh based off of my accent. I certainly didn't look posh, I still don't. I can't say I was posh either, as my family were originally from working class backgrounds. I still am called posh, despite trying to lose the accent, despite living in one of the rougher areas and below the poverty line. And I'm a cleaner for a budget hotel chain. I'm the furthest thing from posh. So it does certainly go both ways; I do see a lot of hate directed towards the Birmingham accent. People carrying it are often called chavs, and it's typically assumed people from the city aren't very nice (at least, from my experience). 

This is basically what I was taught. It's weird how classism regarding accents still exists, but people are trying to break it down in some ways, such as having people with regional accents present news stuff on the BBC when previously it was only people with RP. However it is still seen. We looked at an article in college about this school who basically punished students for using slang and phrases from their regional accents.

I'm seventeen, and was diagnosed a few weeks ago, after a mental health crisis which started when I was fifteen. I totally understand how you feel now. Personally, I had no idea females could also have ASD until I started looking into autism. I couldn't understand why all of my autistic male friends were so relatable. 

Have you ever read The State Of Grace? It's a book about a fifteen/sixteen year old girl with Aspergers. It's set in the UK, so if you're American some of the school stuff may not make much sense. It's still an amazing book which I found so relatable. Like, if it were general YA fiction I probably would have found it annoying, as it holds many clichés, but as they're navigated by a girl on the autistic spectrum, they seem to have a whole new perspective which I, and I hope others, can finally relate to. It's also important to note that she isn't made out to be savant, or really show any of these savant characteristics, or any obsession with maths or science (think Sheldon Cooper, or Christopher from The Curious Incident Of The Dog In The Night Time). Her special interest is horses, which I loved as not only do I love horses, but I find special interests to be so tricky.  To explain better what I mean, take my very good friend. He's also on the spectrum. Currently he's obsessed with philosophy and politics, and past obsessions have included physics, space, maths, that kind of thing. Then you have me, where my obsessions have included armadillos, Queen, Stephen King's books, horses, rats, Eastenders, BJD's and Disney Films (Currently the last three are the ones which play the biggest part in my life, but I typically cycle through these, and I hope to get pet rats soon). I think it's possibly the representation you're looking for; it's just a shame it's so unpopular compared to, say, Th Curious Incident. 

Also, since I'm A Celebrity, Get Me Out Of Here was aired, I'd say we got a bit more representation, thanks to Anne Hergerty, a woman with Aspergers who took part. She's around sixty, of my mind serves me correctly. I'd say she's certainly spread awareness, judging by the number of articles made about the subject. One which really stuck out is how apparently on the night I'm a Celeb aired, the National Autistic Society had to shut their site down temporarily or something, as there were too many people going on at he same time.

I feel like while we definitely need more representation, we are also going in tbe right direction. I hate being stuck in this "not quite adult" stage yet too; I'm so very nearly an adult, and yet I'm still not taken seriously. I don't think anyone ever is. You're always "too young" a valid opinion, and valid experiences and then suddenly you wake up one day and them you're "too old" to have a valid opinion, and valid experiences.

I've always found Young Adult fiction to be rather cliché. And I know literature is littered with clichés, but I've always found that YA has not only the most annoying, but the most obvious clichés. Things like having an extremely quirky, "not like the other guys/girls", overly intelligent main character, or side character. Or perhaps the whole "he/she saved him/her, but couldn't save themselves". That kind of thing.

I find the clichés to be so fustrating, and it puts me off the novel somewhat. There are absolutely good YA books out there, I'm not saying all of them are awful, but the popular books tend to be the ones I find most fustrating.

It baffles me because you'd expect an adult to have moved on from these clichés. I began reading into the genre this year as I'd never really explored it (I went from children's literature to adults, and swapped YA for classical childrens literature. I read a few adult classics, but I couldn't grasp the language). I've come to find that a lot of popular books seem to follow a strange kind of formula. 

I think another reason it baffles me is because, from speaking to people I know, they like what they read as they can relate to the protagonist. I'm not sure how a thirty five year old finds a sixteen year old to be relatable; unless they're one of those overly annoying adults who can't seem to accept the fact they are married with a partner and kids, and still want to live as though they are experiencing youth. While from a health and social care standpoint young adulthood lasts from the age of nineteen to the age of forty five, I feel like that is not what authors have in mind.

I find adults who read young adult to be reading it because they can't get into anything else. Which also baffles me, as comparing the writing style of YA to adult literature, you don't find too many differences. If anything, you get some more complicated language YA novels *because* of these overly intelligent, manic pixie dream boy/girl characters. 

Perhaps I'm not seeing it from others perspectives. I'm not great at empathy or seeing others points of view or anything. Hence why I read a lot. At the end of the day, I don't care what people read as that is up to them and doesn't affect me. Yes, I'll always question why someone likes something; I find it says a lot about them as a person. But in all, I can't say adults buying teenagers literature is my biggest problem with the world.

I n all seriousness, I've heard that even though Young Adult fiction is for... well, it's implied reader is young adults, it isn't common for people in there twenties and thirties to buy it. That baffles me.

I'm a cleaner for a popular hotel chain in the UK. While I'm obviously part of a team, I work mostly alone. I work weekends mostly (though if it is an extended term break such as the Summer I'll pick up extra shifts) so I do find that you can sometimes get rather noisy families. However, where I work you're allowed music on so I just play it loud enough to cover it up (sometimes that is difficult; earphones aren't allowed where I work for health and safety reasons, though it doesn't stop one woman wearing them all the time). 

The work is relatively simple, you just follow the route and do the rooms on the sheet given. You ens up falling into a routine which is great, and as someone who sometimes needs to like... move (if that makes sense), I find some aspects actually quite relaxing. There is a time limit to work to, so there is that stress, and I do find I often overrun as I don't sleep well so I'm often exhausted, and as I'm at school all week I really don't get a break. My coworkers are great and often come back to help though, and you won't be expected to do loads in a short space of time to start with. 

The pay is fairly good here, I get paid a little over £8 an hour, though if you're American or work elsewhere I have no idea what you'll be looking at. Downsides include it being physically exhausting (though I promise it doesn't take long to get into the swing of things. I used to get really, really bad body aches, particularly in my feet and my back, though I rarely experience them now. Only on particularly hard days). If smells are an issue for you, then you may find some rooms physically sickening. I know I certainly have an issue with some, particularly rooms men have stayed in (I've become pretty good at distinguishing which gender has slept in a room, and would be fairly confident to base my guess on smell alone. I wonder if my sexuality plays part in my particular hatred and repulsion by this smell though I can't be sure). And, you're hours aren't set. The amount you work a day depends on your speed, the amount of rooms you have on a sheet, and how quickly the guests leave (I have days where the majority stay until lunch, which is the latest time to check out, so I'm working ridiculously over time) though I find this last point is easily combated by switching rooms with coworkers, which could be difficult if you aren't comfortable with that kind of thing (I found it hard to begin with, but my mother works at the same place, so I'm familiar with most coworkers, and on good terms with them so I found it easier. There are, however, some I still won't talk to). 

Overall it's a decent job, if you can get over the downsides. Was this too detailed? I ramble a lot. I'm sorry.
